title.en: Coyote and Buffalo: Why There Are No Buffalo in the West
title.zh: 郊狼與野牛：西部何以無野牛

region.en: Plains east of the Salish country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩利什故地以東之平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (8) Coyote and Buffalo' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Coyote urinates on the skull of a dead buffalo-bull and is chased at full speed by the living bull — 'Because you urinated on my head while I was dead.' He makes peace, sharpens the bull's horns with pitchy pine points, and helps him kill the rival who took his wives; the grateful bull gives him a fat buffalo-cow to wife with the rule that he must not sleep with her for three nights. Coyote breaks the rule, loses her, wins her back, kills and eats her as she comes up a defile — and then cannot defecate himself, so the meat-eating birds and animals strip the carcass while he stands helpless and Wolverene runs off with the pelvic bones. Had he carried his wife home, there would now be buffalo all over the Okanagon country; buffaloes do not go farther west than the place where Coyote killed his wife, and since the marrow was spilled on the water, some lakes have oil on their surface.
summary.zh: 郊狼溺於死牛頭骨之上，活牛狂奔而來復仇：『爾於吾死時辱吾首！』郊狼求和，以松脂尖為其磨角，助其誅殺奪妻之敵。牛以肥母牛妻之，惟誡：『三夜不得同寢。』郊狼破戒失妻，復得之，後竟於峽谷中射殺烹食；而己卻腹脹難便，百鳥百獸群集而食，狼獾更銜其骨而去。若其攜妻還家，則今奧卡諾根之地當遍野牛。野牛西行至郊狼殺妻之處而止；髓脂瀉入水中，故今有湖面浮油。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling about, and went northward from the Salish to the Blackfoot country. He found the skeleton of an old buffalo-bull, urinated on the skull, and passed on. Presently he heard a noise like wind behind him; he looked back but saw nothing. The noise grew louder, and he looked again: a buffalo-bull was approaching at full speed — it was the bull whose skull he had insulted. Coyote ran away, but the Buffalo gained on him; he ran round and round a large bowlder until exhausted, and shouted, 'Why do you chase me?' The Buffalo replied, 'Because you urinated on my head while I was dead.' 'What killed you?' — 'I became old, and a younger bull killed me. My horns were dull.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 76-77 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote said, 'If you will promise not to hurt me, I will sharpen your horns after I have had a rest.' Buffalo stopped. Coyote gathered pitchy roots of the yellow pine, which have sharp points, and attached them to the ends of Buffalo's horns, then told him to go toss an old log to test them. Buffalo did as directed, and his horns stood the test. He was very glad, and said, 'I will be your friend. My rival, who took my wives, is somewhere around. Let us go and find him! I will kill him and take back the women, and will give some of them to you.' On the plain they found Buffalo's enemy surrounded by a band of women; Buffalo tore him in two, and said to Coyote, 'Friend, pick out one of these women, whichever you like.' Coyote asked for a fat one, 'for my home is far away, and she will get thin while travelling with me.' Buffalo picked out a very fat one, and said, 'This one will be your wife. You must not sleep with her for three nights. After that everything will be well.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 77 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote started homeward with his new wife. The second night he said to himself, 'The time that he named is too long. No one since the beginning of the world has had a wife for three nights without sleeping with her' — and she became invisible and returned to her band. He went back and found Buffalo-Bull, who was angry but forgave him, giving her back with the reminder, 'Now you must remember, three days.' This time was sufficient to cross the mountains; then he lay with his wife and was glad. On the succeeding day he was hungry, and thought how fat she was: 'My wife is only a trouble to me. I will kill and eat her.' He sent her up a defile, ran around the hill, met her coming up, shot her twice from above, and cut her up — she was very fat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 77-78 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Coyote tried to defecate, but could not; he was seized with violent pains and could not stand up. Magpie came and alighted on the carcass, then Eagle, Buzzard and Raven, all the birds that eat meat; Wolf came, and all the animals that eat meat, and they ate the buffalo-cow while Coyote could only call them nasty names. The bones were picked clean and scattered; Wolverene stuck his head into the pelvic bones and ran away with them. At last Coyote passed a little dung, was angry at his excrement, beat it flat on a rock, and blamed it for the loss of the fine meat. He found some bones, cooked and broke them, filled his wife's bladder with the marrow and set it in a lake to cool — and when Muskrat swam past he scared it for fun, until it ducked its head suddenly and tore the bladder, spilling all the marrow, which Coyote could not catch. The foolish Coyote had lost both his wife and his meat. Had he been wise and carried his wife home, there would now be buffaloes all over the Okanagon country. Buffaloes do not go farther west than the place where Coyote killed his wife; and since the marrow was spilled on the water, some lakes have on their surface oil, or something that appears like oil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 78-79 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Grizzly-Bear's home across the river (symbolic pin at Okanagon River)
region.zh: 河彼岸灰熊之家（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Collected by Franz Boas; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (10) Coyote and Grizzly-Bear' (Okanagon, collected by Boas)

summary.en: Coyote's eldest son goes to marry Grizzly-Bear's daughter; the Bear steps on his arrow-points, sends him to shoot a bear from below, and the bear kills him. The second son fares the same. The youngest makes two stone-pointed arrows, stands above the bear instead of below, shoots it twice, cuts off its head, and throws it into his father's tent, where Coyote tests the mourners by producing stone, dung and a little bush from himself as the Bear investigates the laughter. Finally Coyote escapes over a river-log he has secretly had the Wood-worm riddle through the middle — Grizzly-Bear follows his directions, and the log breaks under him in midstream.
summary.zh: 郊狼長子往娶灰熊之女；熊踐其箭鏃，遣其自下射熊，熊反殺之。次子亦然。幼子製石鏃箭二支，居高位而射，二箭斃熊，割其首擲入父帳。熊聞笑聲入帳察看，郊狼先後化石、化糞、化小灌木戲之。最後郊狼賄木蠧蟲暗蛀過河之木，佯稱木堅；灰熊依其言踏木過河，至中流木斷墜水。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative collected by Boas (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote lived with his children. His eldest son said, 'Father, I am going to see the daughter of Grizzly-Bear.' He made arrows and started. When he arrived, the Bear said, 'Have you arrived, son-in-law?' He told his daughter to go to dig roots, then went out and stepped on the arrow-points of the son-in-law. He said, 'Come, son-in-law, shoot for me that bear, that I may eat it!' — and told him, 'Stand below the bear and shoot it.' Coyote's son went and shot at the bear, which pursued him and killed him. Coyote's second son found out what had happened, made arrows, went to marry the Grizzly-Bear's daughter, and was killed in the same way as his elder brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 79 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally the youngest son went. He made two arrows with stone points and said, 'Father, I shall go to find out what happened to my brothers.' When he arrived, the Bear said, 'Have you arrived, son-in-law?' and sent his daughter to dig roots; then went out and stepped on the weapons of his son-in-law. 'Come, son-in-law, shoot that bear for me, that I may eat it!' The boy took his arrows and sat down in his canoe, crossed the river, climbed the hill, and stood above the bear. He went down towards the bear and shot it; he shot it again, and the bear rolled down. He ran after it and cut off its head, then sat down in his canoe and went down the river to his father's tent, throwing the head into the tent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 79-80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Bear came and heard the people laughing, he entered and saw a stone on the floor; he was going to bite it, but said, 'No, my teeth will break,' and went out again. After he had gone some distance he heard laughter, turned back, and saw dung on the floor: 'No, it is very bad.' Again he heard laughter and entered; there was a little bush which scratched him. Then Coyote jumped out laughing and ran away, and the Bear pursued him. Coyote transformed himself into a bush; the Bear went on, saw the bush, and Coyote laughed at him from a distance. Again pursued, Coyote transformed himself into a stick; the Bear saw it and said, 'This is a nice stick.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: I will use it as a walking-stick' — then, 'No, it is too heavy. I will leave it,' and dropped it. Still pursued, Coyote walked over a log that lay across a river; he paid the Wood-worm and said, 'Make a hole in the middle of this log that lies across the river.' When Grizzly-Bear arrived he asked which way Coyote had gone, and Coyote replied, 'I came over this log. Is it strong? Yes, it is very strong. Come!' The Bear jumped on the log and was walking along; when he reached the middle of the stream, the log broke in the middle, and he fell into the water. Then Coyote went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote's Work Finished: The Chief Comes Down
title.zh: 功成身退：主神下凡驗工

region.en: Okanagon country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 2. Old-One' (Coyote's rest and return; Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Coyote transforms the good ancients into Indian pairs settled across the country with different names and languages — the ancestors of the tribes — and teaches people to eat, dress, build, hunt and fish; but he is too fond of tricks, often selfish, boastful, vain and foolish, and duped by those he meant to dupe. When his work is done, the Chief comes down as a poor old man, challenges the boastful traveller ('If you are Chief, take that lake and place it yonder' — Coyote does it, but cannot put it back), and dismisses him to a prepared home: Coyote disappears, and no one knows where he is. The Chief will return with all the spirits of the dead when the Earth-Woman is very old; then the Earth-Woman will revert to her natural shape and live as a mother among her children, and there will be much happiness.
summary.zh: 郊狼化善古者為印第安夫妻，散居各地，賜以族名與語言——諸族之祖；又教民飲食、衣著、築屋、狩獵、捕魚。然其性好戲謔，時而自私自誇，愚而受騙。功成之際，主神化身貧老下凡相驗：『汝若主神，能移彼湖否？』郊狼移之，卻不能復位；主神一移即回。乃曰：『汝功已成，行遠勞苦，善事亦多。今有居所為汝備矣。』郊狼遂隱，無人知其所在。主神言：待大地之母極老之時，彼將偕亡者諸靈重返；屆時大地復為母親之身，與兒女同樂，萬事皆善。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Eschatological closing of the Coyote mission cycle; the informant's narration includes Christian elements noted by Teit. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote then travelled on the earth, and did many wonderful things. He destroyed the powers of all the monsters and evil beings that preyed on the people. He transformed the good ancients into Indians, and divided them into groups or pairs, and settled them in different places; for the Chief desired the earth to be inhabited everywhere, and not only in a few places. He gave each people a different name and a different language. These pairs were the ancestors of all the present Indian tribes; and that is why there are so many Indian tribes and languages now, and why Indians live all over the country. He taught the people how to eat, how to wear clothes, make houses, hunt, fish, and more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 82 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote did a great deal of good, but he did not finish everything properly. Sometimes he made mistakes; and although he was wise and powerful, he did many foolish things. He was too fond of playing tricks for his own amusement; he was also often selfish, boastful, and vain; he sometimes overreached himself, and occasionally was duped by persons whom he intended to dupe. He was ugly, and women generally did not like him; he often used cunning to gain his ends. He was immortal, and did not die as we die. Coyote had done nearly everything he could think of, and was travelling from place to place to learn of other things that remained to be done. Chief looked over the earth, and said, 'Coyote has now done almost everything that he is capable of doing. I will relieve him.' Chief came down, and travelled in the shape of a poor old man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 82-83 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He met Coyote, who said to him, 'I am Coyote. Who are you?' Chief answered, 'I am Chief of the earth. It was I who sent you to set the world right.' Coyote said, 'No, you never sent me. I don't know you. If you are Chief, take that lake and place it yonder.' Chief said, 'No. If you are the wonderful Coyote, let me see you do it!' Coyote did it. Chief said, 'Place it back again.' Coyote tried, but could not do it; he thought this strange. Chief placed it back. Coyote said, 'Now I know you are Chief.' Chief said, 'Your work is finished. You have travelled far and long, and done much good. Now, you shall go to where I have prepared a home for you.' Coyote disappeared, and no one knows where he is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 83 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Chief prepared to leave also. He said, 'I will send messages to earth by the souls of people that reach me, but whose time to die has not come. They will carry messages to you from time to time; and when their souls return to their bodies, they will revive, and tell you their experiences. Coyote and myself will not be seen again until the Earth-Woman is very old. Then we shall return to earth, for it will require a new change by that time. Coyote will precede me by some little time; and when you see him, you will know that the time is at hand. When I return, all the spirits of the dead will accompany me, and after that there will be no spirit-land. All the people will live together. Then will the Earth-Woman revert to her natural shape, and live as a mother among her children. Then will things be made right, and there will be much happiness.' The Earth-Woman is now very old, and even her bones (the rocks) are crumbling away; therefore the time cannot be far away when the earth will be transformed again, and when the spirits of the dead will come back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 83-84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Creation: The Man Who Was Also a Wolf

region.en: Similkameen country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Princeton)
region.zh: 西米爾卡米恩故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於普林斯頓）

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 3. The Creation' (Okanagon, from Similkameen)

summary.en: The Chief above made the earth, small at first, letting it increase and rolling it out until it was very large; he covered it with a white dust that became the soil. He made three worlds, one above another — the sky world, the earth we live on, and the underworld — all connected by a pole or tree that passes through the middle of each. Then he created the animals, and at last a man who was also a wolf; from this man's tail he made a woman. These first people, called 'Tai'en' by the old people who knew the story well, were the ancestors of all the Indians.
summary.zh: 上界主神造大地，初甚小，任其增大，輾轉鋪展至廣；覆以白塵，即為土壤。又造三界，上下相疊——天界、人間、冥界——中有神柱（或神樹）貫通。後造百獸，終造一人，其身亦狼；自此人之尾造出一女。二人乃初民，古之知者稱之為『Tai'en』，印第安諸族皆其後裔。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon (Similkameen) creation narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Chief above made the earth. It was small at first, and he let it increase in size. He continued to enlarge it, and rolled it out until it was very large. Then he covered it with a white dust, which became the soil. He made three worlds, one above another — the sky world, the earth we live on, and the underworld. All are connected by a pole or tree which passes through the middle of each. Then he created the animals. At last he made a man, who, however, was also a wolf. From this man's tail he made a woman. These were the first people. They were called 'Tai'en' by the old people, who knew the story well, and they were the ancestors of all the Indians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of the Earth and People: The Red Earth of the Indians
title.zh: 大地與人民之始：紅土造印第安人

region.en: Okanagon Lake country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 4. Origin of the Earth and People' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: The Chief made seven worlds, of which the earth is the central one — three above, three below (some say the first priests or white people told us this, but some of us believe it now). He stretched the earth out with its head to the west: the west is the head of the earth, the place of the dead, and the direction the great rivers flow and the souls take, following the course of the waters. Perhaps in the beginning the earth was a woman: the Chief stretched her body across the world, feet east and head west, transformed her into the earth we live on, and made the first Indians out of her flesh, the soil — out of balls of red earth or mud, which is why we are reddish-colored. Other races were made from soil of different colors, and their mingling accounts for the intermediate shades; and as red earth is more nearly related to gold and copper, the Indians are nearer to gold and finer than other races.
summary.zh: 主神造七界，人間居中——上三下三（或云此說出自初來之傳教士與白人，然今亦有人信之）。神鋪展大地，首在西：西方乃大地之首、亡者之鄉，大河西流，魂魄亦隨水西去。或謂太初大地本為女子：神展其身橫亙世界，足東首西，化其為大地；又取其肉（即土壤）搓紅泥為丸，造出第一批印第安人——故吾儕膚色微紅。他族以異色之土造成，諸族相遇雜處，遂生中間膚色。紅土與金銅同氣，故印第安人近金而貴於他族。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Chief (or God) made seven worlds, of which the earth is the central one. There are three worlds above, and three below. Maybe the first priests or white people told us this, but some of us believe it now. When the Chief made the earth, he stretched it out with its head to the west; therefore the west is the head of the earth. Heaven, or the place of the dead, is in that direction, and the great rivers all flow westward. West is the direction the souls take; some say they follow the course the waters take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Perhaps in the beginning the earth was a woman. Some Indians say so, and state that the Chief stretched her body across the world (probably the water), and that she lay with her feet east and her head west. He transformed her into the earth we live on, and he made the first Indians out of her flesh (which is the soil). Thus the first Indians were made by him from balls of red earth or mud, and this is why we are reddish-colored. Other races were made from soil of different colors. Afterwards some of these different races met at certain points and intermingled, and thus the intermediate shades of color have arisen. As red earth is more nearly related to gold and copper than other kinds of earth, therefore the Indians are nearer to gold, and finer than other races.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: War with the Sky People: The Chain of Arrows Broken

region.en: Okanagon Lake country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 5. War with the Sky People' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: The people resolve to make war on the Sky people — some say to procure fire from there — and Grizzly-Bear, their chief, calls everyone to shoot arrows at the sky; all fall short, even Fish, Snakes and Toads. Only Chickadee is left, and no one expects him to hit — but his arrow strikes the sky. In turn the others shoot arrows into each nock until a chain reaches the ground, and up it they climb, leaving only Grizzly-Bear and Black-Bear, who quarrel over who shall climb next, chase each other around the ladder, and knock it down. In the sky the attackers are defeated and flee; finding the lower part of the chain gone at mid-descent, they hesitate, the crowd above breaks the ladder with its weight, and all fall — those left above kill themselves in the drop, the rest are killed by the Sky people, and the Fish fare worst: Sucker broke all his bones.
summary.zh: 族人欲征天族（或云為奪火），熊酋召眾射天；眾箭皆墮，魚、蛇、蟾亦然。最後唯剩山雀，人皆不望其能中——然其箭竟釘天。於是眾輪流以箭續射，鏈成及地，攀之登天；僅灰熊與黑熊未上，因爭先後而追逐，竟撞倒箭梯。天上攻者敗退；退至半空，發覺下段箭鏈已失，猶豫不敢跳，而上空人潮愈擠愈重，箭梯竟斷，全體墜落——空中餘者躍下自斃，其餘為天族所誅。魚類最慘，胭脂魚遍體骨碎。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Arrow-chain ascent to the sky, a widespread Plateau motif. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time the people wanted to make war on the Sky people (some informants say they wanted to procure fire from there). Grizzly-Bear, who was chief, called all the people together to shoot arrows at the sky. Each animal and bird shot, but all the arrows fell short. The Fish, Snakes, and Toads also tried. At last only Chickadee (or Wren?) was left, and no one expected that he could hit the sky; Coyote said he did not need to try, when he himself had failed. However, Chickadee's arrow hit the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The others all shot in turn again, and Chickadee shot an arrow which stuck in the nock of the first one. They kept on shooting until a chain of arrows had been made which reached the ground, and on this they climbed to the sky. Grizzly-Bear and Black-Bear only remained. They quarrelled as to who should climb next: Black-Bear said Grizzly was too heavy and would break the ladder. They chased each other around the ladder, and finally knocked it down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile the people who had reached the sky had attacked the people there, and had been defeated. They fled; and when the first ones reached the hole in the sky, they descended one after another. When they reached half way down, they found the lower part gone, and hesitated to drop so far. Meanwhile the people crowded so thickly on the ladder above that their weight broke it, and they all fell down. Those left above threw themselves down and killed or hurt themselves, while the remainder were killed by the Sky people. The Fish, who had no wings, fared worst: Sucker broke all his bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Dirty-Boy: Sun Descends to Wed the Chief's Daughter
title.zh: 髒小子：太陽下凡娶酋長之女

region.en: Large camp of the Okanagon country (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地大營（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 6. Dirty-Boy' (Okanagon)

summary.en: The chief's two beautiful daughters have refused every suitor, and Sun and Star, brother and sister in the sky, descend to test them — Sun as a dirty, sore-eyed boy, Star as a decrepit grandmother, in a ruined mat lodge at the camp's edge. In the shooting contest the disguised boy kills the eagle through his lodge-door while Coyote misses twice and is stripped of his extra arrows; in the fisher-trapping contest his two willow dead-falls by the lodge-door hold the only two prime fishers, while Coyote's ten traps catch nothing. The chief keeps his word, but one daughter detours to marry Raven's ugly eldest son; the other attends the 'sick, dying' boy as commanded, and on the third night Sun and Star resume their true forms — a skin lodge richer than the Blackfeet's, a copper kettle, a woman clothed in stars, and a man whose hair shines like sun-rays. The rejected sister falls four times trying to walk the golden-dust trail, and when game grows scarce Sun turns over dried droppings on the plain until every one becomes living game driven into the chief's pit — the last, a gaunt steer that is nearly all fat. The steer-hairs become cattle; the wise sister's line prospers and the foolish one is shamed.
summary.zh: 酋長二美拒不嫁，太陽與星（天上兄妹）下凡試之：太陽化為目爛身污之小兒，星化為襤褸老嫗，營邊搭破爛草席之屋。射雕之賽，髒小子於門內發箭連中雕心；郊狼兩射皆空，多箭被奪。捕貂之賽，老嫗於門旁置柳木陷阱二，竟得毛色一明一暗之上等貂二張；郊狼十陷無獲。酋長守諾，令二女下嫁；長姊途徑渡鴉家入而嫁其醜子，幼妹守命侍『病篤』之夫。第三夜，兄妹復本相：帳化皮帳華過黑腳族，釜化銅釜，老嫗星衣熠熠，男兒髮光如日。被拒之姊四度踏上金塵之路而四度跌倒。獵物匱乏之時，太陽翻轉原上乾糞，糞皆化活獸，驅入酋長深坑；最後一頭瘦牛，剖之幾全為脂。牛毛化家牛，故今家畜多於野獸；賢姊之後昌，愚姊蒙羞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Celestial bridegroom tale (star-husband cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people of a certain region were living together in a very large camp. Their chief had two beautiful daughters of marriageable age; many young men had proposed to them, but all had been refused. The chief said, 'Whom do my daughters wish to marry? They have refused all the men.' Sun and Star, who were brother and sister, lived in the sky, and had seen all that had happened. Sun said to his sister, 'The chief's daughters have rejected the suits of all our friends. Let us go down and arrange this matter! Let us try these girls!' They made clothes, and at night descended to earth, erecting a lodge on the outskirts of the camp with the appearance of being very old and belonging to poor people — old poles, tattered tule-mat covering, beds of dried brush, kettles and cups of poorly made bark. Star had assumed the form of a decrepit old woman dressed in rags, and Sun that of a dirty boy with sore eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 85-86 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief resolved to find husbands for his daughters, announcing a shooting contest in four days: an eagle would perch on the tall tree, and whoever killed it should have the chief's daughters. Coyote was there and felt happy, thinking he would win the prize; the previous evening Sun had begged his 'grandmother' to make him a bow and arrows, and Star, taking pity, cut a red willow branch for a bow and some twigs for arrows, strung with a poor string and unfeathered. In the morning the eagle alighted on the tree. Coyote shouted, 'I will shoot first. Watch me hit the eagle' — his arrow struck the lowest branch and fell, and the people laughed; his second fell short, and when he tried to shoot all his arrows the people seized him, saying, 'You are allowed to shoot twice only.' All the people shot and missed. Then Sun said, 'Grandmother, lift the door of the lodge a little, so that I can shoot' — 'First get out of bed!' She pulled the mat aside a little, and he shot: the first arrow hit the tail of the eagle, the second pierced its heart. Wolf shouted that he had shot the bird from the lodge-door, but the old woman Star ran faster, picked it up, and carried it to the chief, claiming his daughters for her grandson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 86-87 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the people made fun of Dirty-Boy — 'He is bedridden. He defecates and urinates in his bed. He is lousy, sore-eyed, and scabby-faced' — and the chief, loath to give his daughters to such a person, announced one last contest: each man to set two traps for fishers, one a light one and one a dark one, both prime skins. Sun asked his sister, 'Grandmother, make two traps for me' — 'First get out of bed!' — but she had pity and made two dead-falls of willow sticks, which he had set one on each side of the lodge-door. When all the men returned by noon, not one had caught a fisher; Star found two fine fishers in the traps and dragged them to the chief, saying, 'I hear you asked for two fishers; here are two that my grandson caught.' Coyote, who had boasted and carried ten traps instead of two, had got nothing, and angrily called Dirty-Boy 'Defecate-in-Bed' and 'Urinate-in-Bed.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 87 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief said to his daughters, 'You must become the wives of Dirty-Boy. I tried to save you by having two contests; but since I am a great chief, I cannot break my word. Go now, and take up your abode with your husband.' On the way they had to pass Raven's house, where the Ravens were laughing. The elder sister went in and became the wife of Raven's eldest son — ugly, with a big head, but she thought it better than to marry a dirty, sickly boy. The younger went on and sat down by Dirty-Boy's side, and the old woman told her, 'Your husband is sick, and soon he will die. He stinks too much. You must not sleep with him. Go back to your father's lodge every evening; but come here in the daytime, and watch him and attend him.' The Raven family, angry that she had not entered their house, dressed their new daughter-in-law in their finest — a dress covered with beads, shells, elk's teeth and quill-work, a jade celt at her belt; the younger sister paid no attention, but returned every morning to gather fire-wood and attend her sick husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 87-88 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening of the third day Sun said to his sister, 'We will resume our true forms to-night, so that the people may see us to-morrow.' That night they transformed themselves: the old mat lodge became a fine new skin lodge, surpassing those of the Blackfeet, richly decorated with streamers tied to the top and painted; the old bark kettle became a bright copper kettle; the old woman became a fine-looking person of tall figure, her clothes covered with shining stars; and Dirty-Boy became a young, handsome man of light complexion, his clothes covered with shining copper, his hair reaching to the ground and shining like the rays of the sun. In the morning the people said, 'Some rich chief has arrived, and has camped where the poor people were.' When the girl arrived and was told 'Come in and sit with your husband!' she knew who the woman was, and saw the handsome man reclining, his garments and hair decorated with bright suns; then she was glad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 88-89 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sun took his wife to the copper kettle at the door, which contained a shining liquid, and pushed her head into it; when the liquid ran down over her hair and body, lines of sparkling small stars formed on her. He told her to empty the kettle, and as the liquid ran to the chief's lodge it formed a path as of gold-dust: 'This will be your trail when you go to see your father.' Now the people had eaten most of their winter provisions, and the hunters could kill no game; Sun told his wife to have her father make many pits for capturing game. As she walked the shining trail, her sister ran out of Raven's house intending to pass herself off as the other wife of Dirty-Boy, and tried to walk on the trail — but four times she fell. Sun went out on the plain, gathered up the dried excrement of game, and turned each one over, and it became alive; he did this with several hundred, then took a whip and drove all the game into the chief's deep pit, where they were killed as they fell. The last animal had originated from a very large dropping: a large, lean steer, nearly all fat, with only threads of flesh running through it. Sun took the hairs the chief had saved from the animals' backs and turned them into game again, so that game became plentiful; the four steer-hairs became cattle, and therefore cattle are more plentiful than game at the present day. Since this time some chiefs' daughters have been wise, others foolish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 89-90 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bear-Woman: Rescue from the Grizzly's Cave

region.en: Lily-patch and cliff-cave, Similkameen country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西米爾卡米恩故地百合田與崖洞（象徵定位）

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 7. The Bear-Woman' (Okanagon, from Similkameen)

summary.en: While her husband hunts, a woman digging lily-roots is seized by a Grizzly-Bear — 'I want you to be my wife' — and carried to his cave-house. Her husband searches; tracks show the bear left with her but none of her own. On the fourth night she appears in his dream with full instructions: arrows anointed with snake-fat and rattlesnake-poison, a seat on the prepared bowlder, and on the fourth morning, when she circles digging past the rock, to shoot the bear in the throat. The hunter aims at his wife to make her cry out 'Husbands never kill their wives!'; the enraged Bear turns to look, and takes the poison arrow in the throat, dying as the second arrow's shaft falls away. The wife swoons through the Bear's dying power, and is only saved by washing with fir-tops and konelp; she must be kept apart in a fir-brush lodge, fed and washed by her sisters-in-law, until next spring, when she returns to her husband's lodge as before.
summary.zh: 獵人外出，其妻掘百合根時遭巨熊擄走——『吾欲汝為妻』——帶回崖洞。夫尋妻不獲，見熊跡而無人跡。第四夜妻入夢授計：蛇脂與響尾蛇毒塗箭，預坐巨石之後；第四日晨，妻繞石掘根而過，射熊咽喉。獵人先瞄其妻，逼其呼『丈夫豈能殺妻！』；熊怒回首，毒箭正中咽喉，第二箭發，箭桿脫落，熊斃。妻因熊死之魔力昏厥，非以冷杉嫩枝與 konelp 洗身不能救。須別居冷杉枝棚，由姑姊妹餵食洗浴，至來春雪融，方得重返夫帳。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon (Similkameen) narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: It was late fall, and people were in the mountains hunting. Six people were living together — a man and his wife, his parents, and his two sisters. One day when out hunting, the man came on a patch of lily-roots, and on his return told his wife they would move there so she could dig them. They set up a lodge near the place, and on the following morning he showed his wife the spot and left her there to dig. In the afternoon a large Grizzly-Bear appeared. The woman was intent on her work and did not notice the Bear until he was close to her. He said to her, 'I want you to be my wife.' She agreed, for she knew he would kill her if she refused. He took her on his back and carried her to his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 90 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Towards evening the hunter returned carrying a load of deer-meat, but his wife was not there; he searched until dark. At daybreak he went out again, and saw the tracks of the Grizzly-Bear going away, but no tracks of his wife leaving the spot. His father said, 'The Grizzly-Bear has not killed her: he has married her.' The man could neither sleep nor eat, until the fourth night, when his wife appeared to him in a dream and said, 'The Grizzly has taken me.' She told him where the Bear's house was, and gave her instructions: 'He is very fierce and endowed with magic power. You must fix your arrows as I direct you, and sit where I tell you... Prepare medicine to wash me with, for otherwise, when the Bear dies, I shall die too through his power. Prepare one arrow by rubbing it with fat of snakes, and the other arrow anoint with rattlesnake-poison. Sit down on the rock in the place that I have prepared; and on the fourth morning, when I bring the Bear past close to the rock, shoot him in the throat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 90-91 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter made two new arrows with detachable foreshafts and good stone heads, anointed with snake-fat and rattlesnake-poison. The Grizzly-Bear's house was a cave in a cliff, and at daybreak on the fourth morning he saw smoke coming from a hole in the top of the cliff; soon his wife and the Bear emerged. Her face was painted, and she carried her root-digger. When she made the fourth circle of digging and passed quite close to the rock, the hunter aimed an arrow at his wife, and she cried, 'Husbands never kill their wives!' He lowered his bow and laughed. The Bear stood up and was angry, abusing the woman; just then he was close to the rock. The hunter spoke to him, and as the Bear turned to look at him, he shot him right in the throat. The Grizzly tried to pull out the arrow but could remove only the shaft; he rushed at the hunter but could not reach him, and the hunter's second arrow was shot with such great force that the shaft fell off. The Bear fell over and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 91-92 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then his wife swooned, and would have died through the Bear's power, had not her husband rubbed her with fir-tops and konelp. She revived and stood up, and said, 'I warn you not to have connection with me. The influence of the Bear is still over me. Build a lodge of fir-brush for me some distance away from the people. Let your sisters feed me, and wash me with fir and Veratrum-leaves. You may speak to me from a distance. Next spring, when the snow is almost gone, I shall be your wife again.' In the spring she washed at a stream, using hot water, and her sisters-in-law rubbed her with fir-boughs; the hunter also washed. Then she went into his lodge, and lived with him as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 92 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Eagle and Beaver Steal the Fire

region.zh: 哥倫比亞河魚梁（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Franz Boas; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 8. Eagle and Beaver' (Okanagon, collected by Boas)

summary.en: A fragment of the fire-theft cycle: Eagle plans the raid — 'Go to the fish-weir and pretend to be dead, so that they will carry you into the house. I will go, and you shall take some of the fire. Then run away.' Beaver floats to the weir, is caught and carried into the house and skinned; while every man runs out to shoot the eagle overhead, the skinless Beaver seizes the fire, jumps into the water, and swims home with the Eagle flying above him, and they arrive in their country.
summary.zh: 盜火之一節：鷹定計——『汝詐死漂至魚梁，彼等必抬爾入屋；吾隨後至，爾乘亂取火而逃。』狸依計漂至魚梁，被擒入屋剝皮；眾人見空中之鷹，奔出射之。無皮之狸趁隙奪火，躍入水中游回，鷹翔其上，二獸安然抵鄉。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon fragment collected by Boas (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Boas notes it is a fragment of the widespread theft-of-fire story. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Eagle said, 'Go to the fish-weir and pretend to be dead, so that they will carry you into the house. I will go, and you shall take some of the fire. Then run away. We will take it back to our home.' The Beaver went to the fish-weir. They caught him and carried him into the house. They skinned him. Then one man said, 'Look here! There is an eagle. Shoot that eagle.' All the men went out, and the Beaver took the fire and ran away with it. The Beaver jumped into the water and swam back. The Eagle flew above him, and they arrived in their country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 92 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地河岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Franz Boas; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 9. The Mouse' (Okanagon, collected by Boas)

summary.en: The Mouse lived with her children and swam across the river to steal; she was drowned. Her children took the body back into the house and cried over it. After some time a man came and asked why they were crying, and the children replied, 'Oh, we have been crying about what happened in the distant past' — then the children of Mouse laughed.
summary.zh: 鼠母攜兒女而居，恆渡河行竊，終至溺斃。兒女抬屍入屋，哭之。後有一人來問何以哭泣，答曰：『吾等所哭者，乃久遠往事也。』言罷，鼠家兒女皆大笑。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a very short Okanagon tale collected by Boas (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Mouse lived with her children. She swam across the river to steal. She was drowned. Her children took the body back into the house and cried over it. After some time a man came, who said, 'Why are you crying?' The children replied, 'Oh, we have been crying about what happened in the distant past.' Then the children of Mouse laughed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 92 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Skwotilkwola'na: The Fish-Helper and the Cannibal's Tower
title.zh: 斯闊提爾闊拉納：靈魚相助破魔塔

region.en: Lake country of the Similkameen, then the cannibal chief's tower (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西米爾卡米恩湖鄉，後至食人魔高塔（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Kwelte'sqet (Emptying-Cloud), 1904; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 10. Skwotilkwola'na' (Okanagon, from Similkameen)

summary.en: A starving boy of four, fishing from a rotting canoe his parents never saw, hooks a huge, lean tsoqEmu's fish that begs to be released four times, promising that whatever he wishes will appear — 'wish and call my name, which is Skwotilkwola'na.' Fish become plentiful; on the tenth day the fish gives him his name and a dying bay mare staked beyond the hill, whose runty colt he must water and train by grass-whip and widening circles, killing each new colt born of the mare, until the old colt is strong as the wind. With the colt he rides to the cannibal chief's watch-tower, whose maiden daughter plays a flute that sounds by itself; the pretended lame traveller enchants the chief — 'if the girl rode on the horse behind me, the flute would play so beautifully that you also would fall asleep' — and gallops off with her. In the pursuit four grass-stalks speed the horse; then comb (a tract of gulches), clay (a tract of mud), thorn (a thicket of haw-bushes) and water (a lake) are thrown down behind, until the exhausted black horse and its bleeding, torn rider turn back: 'Now I know that you are Skwotilkwola'na; no other could have overcome me.' The boy, later known by his helper's name, wishes a wooden house and garden, and becomes a powerful man.
summary.zh: 四歲貧兒借朽舟垂釣，得瘦長巨魚 tsoqEmu's；魚四度求釋，允諾：『凡有所求，呼我名 Skwotilkwola'na 即可。』自此湖中群魚湧至。第十日，魚以己名與病駒相贈——駒居山後，老駒瘦弱，須以草鞭馴之，繞圈日廣，凡新生之駒皆殺，老駿遂疾如風。少年乘駿往食人魔瞭望塔，其女笛自鳴；佯裝跛旅，以笛聲迷醉魔酋——『若令其女乘我馬後，笛聲更美，君亦將入睡』——遂載女疾馳而逃。追兵漸近，四莖茅草催馬；繼擲木梳化溝壑、擲黏土化泥沼、擲棘刺化山楂叢、擲水化大湖。魔之人馬血污力竭而返：『汝必 Skwotilkwola'na，非此不能勝我。』少年後以其守護靈之名行世，許願得木屋園圃，成一方豪傑。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon (Similkameen) narrative told by Kwelte'sqet in 1904 (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Boas notes the tale is a composite with European tale elements. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: An old man, his wife, and their infant son lived near a lake. They were poor, and food was hard to obtain; they were almost starving. Every day the man went fishing, and the woman dug sxaie'En-roots, finding only a few; her husband caught only a few small fish about four finger-widths in length. Every day the mother washed her son with water in a basket, and carried him on her back when she went root-digging; the boy grew very fast, as all children of the ancients did. When four years old, the boy said, 'I will no longer be carried by my mother. I will accompany my father when he goes fishing.' His father made a line and hooks for him, and took him to the lake, where the boy pointed out an old canoe almost rotted away on the lake-shore that his father had never seen: 'Sit in the bow, and I shall sit in the stern, then we will fish.' As usual, the father caught four small fish, while the boy got none.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 93 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fourth day the boy fished alone, and towards evening cast his line once more and felt a great weight. At last he managed to pull it up, and a large tsoqEmu's-fish came to the surface, its head very large and its body very lean. The fish said, 'Let me go!' but the boy answered, 'I cannot. We are starving. We need you.' The fish repeated the request four times, and finally said, 'If you let me go, you may have anything you wish. As soon as you wish, the object of your desire will appear by your side.' 'True?' — 'True!' They repeated this four times, then the boy let the fish go, which said, 'All you have to do is to wish and call my name, which is Skwotilkwola'na. In ten days I shall see you again.' The fish became plentiful, day by day easier to catch, until on the tenth day he filled the old canoe, and they had enough fish to last a long time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 93-94 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the tenth day, towards evening, the old fish put its head on the gunwale of the canoe and said, 'If you had not let me go, you would never have caught any fish. I will give you my name and my horse. You will find it ten days from to-day standing on the far side of the mountain behind your camp... The horse will give you advice when you need it. Tell no one our name. Meanwhile wash yourself in the water, and run every day for ten days. Do not sleep in your parents' lodge, but build a small lodge near by, and make your bed in it.' Early the next morning he crossed the hill and found an old bay mare staked out, seemingly almost ready to die, her ears hanging down and her jaw-bone loose — with a skoltapi's colt beside her. 'You will find my halter in the bush yonder. Lead me to water. Water me six times, at intervals of seven days. After this the colt will speak to you in my place.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 94 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The colt said, 'You will find my bridle on the bush yonder. Bridle me. Pluck four male stalks of grass... Hit me with them when I tell you to do so... Mount me, and ride me in a small circle four times.' He did as directed, and for each circle he used another blade of grass, and the colt went faster each time. When he returned after seven days, he found the old mare had given birth to a large, fat bay colt, and the old colt looked thin. The latter said, 'Kill the new colt. He kicks me, and I cannot get a suck.' The lad disliked to kill the colt, but obeyed, and each time he returned he found a new colt born, which he killed; each time he rode the old colt in wider circles, and it went faster and faster. The fifth time, the colt said, 'Next time when you come, bring a tiny comb, a thorn from a bush, a little clay wrapped up, and a little water' — and when he called to his helper by the old canoe, 'Grandfather, you promised me your help!', these things appeared under the side of the canoe, the water in a bladder the size of the point of one's finger, the clay wrapped in a piece of skin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 94-95 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fourth run the colt was going like the wind, its mane and tail standing straight out, the noise of its running like a gale of wind in the mountains; it ran the whole course without getting winded, falling, or stumbling, and was now a good-sized horse. 'Now I know I am strong. Let us start on our travels!... We are going a long distance to another country where a cannibal chief lives. He stays at the top of a tall tower, from which he can watch the whole country. His maiden daughter stays in the same house below him. Many have sought her, but the plain is white with their bones. The cannibal kills them with an elk-horn club, and cuts off their heads... The chief's daughter is very fond of music, and spends most of her time playing a flute.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 95 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In due time they came in sight of the chief's house, which towered up like a pillar of smoke. The colt pretended to be a poor, lame traveller; when he came very near, the chief's daughter's flute played by itself, and stopped when he went a distance off. The father came down, curious, and invited the lad in, then went out to look at the colt. 'My horse is always that way. He has magic power. When he comes near any flute, it plays by itself.' Four times the chief offered to buy the horse, but the lad refused. 'If I ride him around four times, the music will play so nicely that your daughter will fall asleep.' He did it, and the girl fell asleep. 'If the girl should ride on the horse behind me, the flute would play so beautifully that you also would fall asleep.' The chief put his daughter on the horse behind the lad, and fell asleep; then the lad rode out of the house and ran his horse like the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 95-96 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they had gone quite a distance, the girl narrated the pursuit — 'Now my father awakes... now he mounts the bay... now he mounts the black. He will surely overtake us and kill us.' The lad pulled a grass-stalk out of his belt and struck his horse, which bounded far ahead; again and again the chief drew near, until the four stalks were used up. Then the lad threw the comb down behind him, and there appeared a tract of gulches separating them from their pursuer; he threw down the clay, and it became a tract of mud; the thorn became a thicket of haw-bushes that tore the chief and his horse; then he threw down the water, and it became a large lake, in which the black horse became exhausted, and the chief had to turn back, calling out, 'Now I know that you are Skwotilkwola'na; no other could have overcome me.' The girl said, 'We are safe. My father has returned. I will now be your wife.' When they reached the lad's home, he was ashamed of the poor house, and went to his helper in the lake, wishing for a wooden house and a garden such as the whites have; he was given these, and he and his wife took up their abode there. He was known afterwards as Skwotilkwola'na, and became a powerful man; the colt disappeared when they reached home — he was only a manifestation of the tsoqEmu's-fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 96-97 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
